What the die takes is the BUFFER STOP, entirely, and the ballast heap and the stack of spare sleepers with it. All three are drawn in the lower left, outside the middle half, and no aim reaches them - the crop has one per cent of freedom and the buffer stop is twenty from the cut. Cheap, and cheaper than it looks: the brief itself set that corner aside for the name band, and a buffer stop is a rail END, which is the one thing this tile is not - it is where a town JOINS the network.

Whole and inside the cut: the board shed with both sliding doors and their diagonal bracing, the stone platform with its timber edge, the water tower on its four braced legs with the swinging spout and the rust in its seams, the hand crane on the platform edge, the crates and the hand barrow.

The focal is the water tower. The shed is a shed and the platform is a platform - at thirty-seven millimetres the tank on its legs is the only POINT on the piece that says railway rather than goods yard, and the track that says it louder is a texture running the width, which is not a thing an eye can land on. It stands whole in the upper right lobe with its conical roof inside the margin, which is what the brief asked for and what this shape needed.

tile-sand-pit.note: The riddle with its screened heap and the leaning shovel, the barrow at the head of the plank run, and the pit between them. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page, so the full WIDTH is kept and 13.4% of the height goes. It is spent off the BOTTOM, not evenly: the focal sits on the riddle, which pulls the window to the top of the page, and that is the right answer here because the bottom of this plate is loose pit floor and the top carries both pieces of furniture that say sand pit rather than hole. Measured rather than guessed - off the bottom keeps 71.1% of the page ink against 70.3% even and 68.2% off the top, and holds the riddle at 100% and the barrow at 87% where a true even spend leaves the barrow at 38%. The band falls on the pit slope, which is sand and nothing else.

tile-butcher.note:
The shambles under its deep overhanging roof: the beam of four hooks, the block, the knife rack, and the salting barrel and trough in front of it. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes, nearly all off the LEFT - the crop keeps x 4.5%-91.1%. The cheapest spend available here: the left of this plate is the raw hide on its rail and the swept flags, and the hide stands in the corner the band covers anyway.

Whole and inside the cut: all four hooks on their beam with daylight between them, which is what says butcher before anything else on the piece does; the chopping block worn hollow in the middle; the knife rack and the saw on the back wall; the salting barrel with its lid off and the scoop standing in the salt. The stone trough loses its front lip to the bottom lobe and still reads as a trough. The hide goes under the band but for its top, and the top is the part that reads - the fold of it hanging over the rail against the light.

The focal is the block. The hooks are the cue, but a row of thin iron is a texture and a texture has no point to land on; the block is the one solid mass in the shaded interior and the hooks hang directly over it, so aiming at one carries the other. Nothing hangs on the hooks and there is no carcass anywhere - the brief asked for that and the plate kept it.

tile-charcoal-kiln.note:
The clamp, its burnt ring and the cordwood stack. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page, so the full width is kept and 13.4% of the height goes. All of it is spent off the BOTTOM, and the subject box is set to the window's exact height so that nothing - not even the focal - can slide it back down. That is the whole decision, and it is worth 9% of the piece: the crown hole is drawn 15% down the page, and a pair's notch descends to a quarter of the tile's height at half-width, so where the crop sits decides whether the hole is in the piece or in the notch. Spent evenly it is cut and the dome is a mound of earth; pinned to the top edge it clears the notch by three per cent of the height and the tile has a chimney again.

What the bottom spend costs is the shovel blade and the front of the finished charcoal, both in the corner the band covers anyway. What the DIE still costs is the dome's left shoulder and the ridge of its apex, which straddle the notch at its deepest - the brick house's lesson wearing turf, and the same rule applies: the tallest thing on the page belongs over a hex peak, a quarter or three quarters across, never over the middle. Here it is at 56% and the crown hole at 60%, which is why one of the two survives and the other does not. Whole and inside the cut: the turf skin with its patches and cracks, all three vent mouths with fire in two of them, the crown hole, the cordwood stack, and the burnt bare ground the clamp stands on.

The focal is the large lit vent under the dome's face. It is the only fire on the piece and the only thing that says burning rather than a heap of earth; the smoke that used to do that job is above the page's own top edge and was never reachable.

tile-clay-pit.note: The pit and the standing water in it, with the clay drying on boards up to the left and the barrow on the ramp to the right. Deliberately NOT the even spend the sand pit gets. Wetness is the whole of what tells this tile from the sand pit at 37 mm, and on the even spend the die left the pool as a sliver in the bottom notch - the two pieces read the same. Dropped the window to a centre of 0.52: the water goes 69% to 78% of its area, and it is paid for out of the drying stack (74% to 66%) and the barrow (59% to 50%). The barrow is the right thing to spend, because a barrow on a plank run is exactly what the sand pit ALSO has - it carries no identifying weight here. The reeds survive whole at every setting, so the second wetness cue costs nothing.

tile-lumber-camp.note: The whole page, for the quarry s reason - a triad window is 0.99 against a square plate and the crop spends nothing. The stacks, the shear legs with the chain and hook, and the lean-to with the crosscut saw all sit in the wide upper band the die keeps; the skid track runs down into the lower lobe under the name band, which is the ground the brief set aside for it. The axe standing in its stump is on the left edge and loses its haft to the cut - it is the one thing here drawn outside the safe box, and it survives as a recognisable axe head.

tile-crop-cotton.note: The whole page - a field is texture edge to edge and there is no object standing in it to protect. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes, and here it is spent off the LEFT, 11.9% off the left against 1.5% off the right. That is the whole of the aiming decision and the PICKING BASKET is what it buys. The basket is drawn well out at the right of the page; a centred crop takes it to the flat edge of the piece and past it, and the left spend brings it inside with the die's full width still under it - it sits between the corner vertices, where a hexagon has not begun to fall away. It is the human evidence on a plate of repeating bushes and it is the thing that tells cotton from any other white-flecked crop at seventeen millimetres, the bolls alone being small pale blobs. What goes off the left is the outermost bushes and bare ridged earth, which is the field again and costs nothing anybody would name. The band falls on dry earth and one bush at the lower left - a bush out of a dozen. Focal on the basket.

tile-crop-flax.note: The whole page, the crop keeping x 6.4%-93.0% and the 13.4% spent EVENLY, because there is no object on this plate at all - only the flower mass - and so nothing a lopsided spend could buy. What decides this tile is not the aim but the READ: flax and grain are both fine upright stems in ruled drills, and the one thing that separates them at seventeen millimetres is the cold slate blue flecked over the whole of this one against the ochre ears of the other. So the crop keeps that flecking edge to edge, which is the entire job, and any spend that traded flower for margin would be the wrong one. The trodden earth along the near edge sits in the lower left where the name band lands on it, which is the ground the brief set aside for it. Focal on the middle of the flower mass - a field of one crop offers no point to prefer, and saying so is more honest than aiming at an arbitrary flower.

tile-crop-grain.note: The whole page. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes, all of it off the RIGHT, and that is the one decision on this tile. It buys the LEFT POPPY. The poppies are the only points on a plate of ruled drills - the brief asked for two or three and got two - and this one is drawn close enough to the left margin that a left spend cuts it outright and a centred one pushes it into the outer twentieth of the piece; the right spend sets it about an eighth of the way in from the flat, clear of the band and legible as a red mark rather than a red pixel. What the spend costs is the outermost column of ears, which is the same ears again. The second poppy survives whole at the lower right, just above the band's end and just above the corner vertex where the hexagon starts to fall away. The stubble and trodden earth along the near edge stay in the lower left, under the name band, which is the ground the brief set aside for it. Focal on the left poppy.

tile-crop-hops.note: The whole page, the crop keeping x 6.4%-93.0% and the 13.4% spent EVENLY - a pole grid repeats and no column of it is worth more than the next, so there is nothing to buy by leaning. The poles run off the TOP edge and are meant to be cut by it, which is the one thing this tile is of: it is the only crop in this game drawn upward, and the height of the poles against every other field is its whole identity. That is also why the composition rule that governs a building does not govern this one - a hop garden drawn to sit inside the top margin would read as a hedge. The die takes the top and bottom points of the page and the poles survive it for exactly that reason, being drawn the full height rather than standing in the middle of it. The band falls on bare trodden earth and a grass tuft at the lower left. Focal on the near pole at its twine ties, the one place where the structure is a point rather than a texture.

tile-crop-vegetables.note: The whole page, the crop keeping x 6.4%-93.0% and the 13.4% spent EVENLY, and here that is a decision rather than a default: both things the brief names besides the cabbages sit at opposite edges - the bean row on crossed poles in the upper left, the leek row in the lower right - so a left spend buys one and cuts the other and a right spend does the reverse. The even spend keeps both, and both then clear the die: the beans below the upper-left diagonal where the hexagon has come out to full width, the leeks just above the lower corner vertex before it falls away again. What it costs is the outer bed on each side, which is more cabbages. The band falls on ridged earth, straw and one cabbage at the lower left - a head out of fifteen, and the affordable kind of loss. Focal on the large central rosette: this tile is of cabbages, and that is the one head big enough to be a point rather than a texture.

tile-dairy.note:
The dairy from its ridge down, with the cheese press, the churn and the turned rounds in front of it. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes. Nearly all of it is spent off the LEFT - the crop keeps x 9.7%-96.3% - and that is the whole of the decision. The left of this plate is grass and the slab-lidded well cover, which is the ground the brief itself set aside for the name band and which the band covers whether the crop takes it or not; the right carries the churn, the pail and the two cheeses, and every one of those is named gear. Measured the other way for comparison: the even spend puts the churn at 81%-97% across the piece, where a single hex has already fallen away, and takes most of it.

Whole and inside the cut: the slated roof and its deep eaves, the open door with the row of shallow setting pans on the slate bench behind it, the press with its stone weight bearing on the cheese in its hoop, and the churn on its stand. The pail loses its foot and the outer cheese its right edge, both to the DIE rather than the crop, and both cheap beside the press.

The focal is the press - the stone weight and the cheese under it. It is the working end and it is the one thing on the plate that tells a dairy from a byre at seventeen millimetres; the building on its own is a low stone shed and could be anything. The band falls on the well cover and the grass round it, which is what the brief drew that corner for.

tile-dock.note:
The jetty on its piles with the boat made fast alongside, and as much of the bank as the band leaves. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes. All of it is spent off the LEFT, and that costs less than it looks - the left of this plate is the bank with the drying rack and the barrel on it, which is the ground the brief itself set aside for the name band, and the band covers that corner whether the crop does or not. Spending right instead would have cut the boat, and after the jetty the boat is what says dock. Whole and inside the cut: the decking and its rail, both bollards, the coiled rope, the chain, and the boat with the net heaped in it and its oar shipped. A fragment of the rack's crossbar survives above the band's top edge; the barrel is under it. Small and timber-built throughout, which is the whole of what keeps this from being read as the harbour.

The focal is the jetty head where the boat is made fast - the working end, and where the eye should land at seventeen millimetres rather than on the open water, which is rather more than half the piece by design.

tile-farm.note: The barn under its thatch, the cart shed with the cart backed into it, the muck heap and the trough, and the yard of ruts between them. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page: full width, 13.4% of the height spent, and the focal on the barn pulls that off the BOTTOM so the thatched ridge keeps its clearance at the top edge. What it costs is the stone trough, which ends up largely under the name band in the lower left. That is a plate-composition cost and not an aiming one: a pair has only vertical freedom, so nothing about the aim can move a thing out of that corner. The barn, the cart and the gate are what the tile is read by, and none of them is in it.

tile-well.note: The wellhead, its shingled roof, the windlass and the bucket over the shaft, with the trough slopping over at the right. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes. It is spent off the LEFT, all of it, and that was worth measuring - centring the crop clips the trough to 79% of its area, and the trough is a named part of this brief and the only thing on the page that shows the well is in use. Spending left instead puts it at 97% and costs the wellhead nothing (97% either way), because the left of this plate is the worn ground and path the brief already marked as expendable. This is the smallest piece in the set at 20.7 x 23.3 mm, which is why the name band takes proportionally the largest bite of any tile here; it falls on that same worn ring.

tile-oil-derrick.note: The lattice derrick and its crown block, the engine house and walking beam, both tanks on their bund, and as much of the slush pit as this shape will carry. A rhombus keeps the upper LEFT and lower RIGHT lobes - the manor's shape, and the manor's problem. The pit is drawn into the lower left, which is both the corner the die cuts and the corner the band covers, so it can never be wholly had. Shifted hard left, and that is measured rather than judged: the pit goes from 43% to 75% of its area and the derrick tower from 95% to 99%, paid for out of the outer tank (100% to 87%, a sliver off its right side). The tower is worth paying for - the brief calls its openwork against the paper the entire silhouette, and it is the only lattice tower in the set. The blackened ground around the well head survives whole and carries the oil where the pit itself is under the band. The upper-left lobe is bare grass: the plate's own empty ground, and no aim reaches it.

tile-market.note:
The shelter, its four posts and the open floor under it. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page: full width, 13.4% of the height spent, taken off the bottom bar two per cent, and all of it foreground flags.

Whole and inside the cut, and this is the whole point of the tile: the daylight going straight through underneath the roof between the posts. The brief calls that gap the entire silhouette and says it must not be closed, and it is the one thing here that no part of the cut touches - it sits in the middle band where a pair keeps its full width. Also whole: all four posts, both trestles, the baskets and the crate stack, the beam scale hung from its tie, and the pole with the rolled awning lashed to it.

What the DIE takes is the finial and the apex of the pyramid roof, drawn at 53% across and 2% down - the notch again. It is the cheapest loss of the five: a hipped roof reads as a hipped roof without its point, and nothing about this piece is being carried by the roofline. The posts and the gap are carrying it.

The focal is under the roof, between the loaded trestle and the hanging scale. There is no door here and no working end - a market is a gap with furniture in it - so the honest place to aim is the middle of the furniture rather than any one piece of it. The band falls on the sacks and the flags at the lower left, which is the ground the brief set aside for it.

tile-mill.note:
The tower, the cap and windshaft, the sails, the tail pole, and the door with its sack hoist over it. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page, so the full WIDTH is kept and 13.4% of the height goes. The subject box is pinned to the top edge of the page so that nothing - not the focal, not the spend - can slide the crop back down, and that pin is the whole decision. It is the charcoal kiln's decision for the charcoal kiln's reason: a pair's notch descends from the top edge to a quarter of the tile's height at half-width, and the cap is drawn 12% down the page centred at 47% across, which is very nearly the worst place on the shape to put it.

Proofed against the alternative rather than argued. Unpinned - subject from 10% down, crop y 7.8%-94.4% - the notch cuts a diagonal bite clean through the cap and the mill loses its head; what that buys is both sacks and the whole millstone, and it is not a trade worth making, because a tower mill without a cap is a stone tower. Pinned, the cap sits as low as the paper allows and keeps its ridge, its boat-shaped body and the windshaft; the notch takes only its front end.

What the pin costs is the two sacks at the step and the foot of the leaning millstone, both of which fall into the BOTTOM notch, and the tail pole's wheel and its track, which go to the lower-left lobe and the band together. The wheel is the real loss - it is what says the cap is turned by hand into the wind - and no aim reaches it: it is drawn at 3%-14% across, outside the safe box on a shape that keeps only its middle half down there.

Whole and inside the cut: the tapering rubble tower and both its small windows, the cap, the windshaft and its hub, the stone doorway with the sack-hoist door above it, the tail pole down its whole length, and the face of the millstone. All four sail arms are still countable from the hub - two of them cut by the top and right edges, which the brief asked for, because cutting them is what makes the mill read as huge.

The focal is the door under the sack hoist. The sails are the silhouette, but a sail is a line and a crop cannot aim at a line; the door is the working end and it sits under the one part of the tower the notch leaves alone.

tile-mine.note: The adit with its cap piece and the tub on the rails in the left lobe, the winding gin over its collared shaft in the right, and the picking table of sorted ore below it. The piece reads ACROSS, which is what the brief asked a pair for and what the plate was drawn to. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page: full width, 13.4% of the height spent, pulled off the bottom by the focal on the adit mouth so the grass above the rise and the adit timbering both keep their clearance. The spoil tip runs out of the lower left under the name band, which is where the brief put it.

spell-fair-wind.note: The full sail with the violet slip across its belly, the bowed mast, the barge, the slack mooring lines on the bollards, the flat water at the hull, the weathervane on the shed pointing the other way, and the straw on the quay that is not moving. 2.2% is trimmed off the BOTTOM (y 2.0%-77.5%) and it takes the near quay planks; every piece of evidence is inside, which is what this box is for - a Fair Wind plate is a list of things that are not doing what the sail is doing, and losing any one of them turns it into a picture of a boat. Focal on the belly of the sail.

spell-farspeak.note: The writing-slope let down on the wagon tail: the open ledger, the pencil lying across the page where it was put down, the pigeonholes of papers behind, and the inkwell with the ink standing up in its ridge. The card keeps y 6.6%-82.0% and nothing is trimmed. Focal on the ridged ink - it is the only thing on the plate that has moved, and it is small, so the box is drawn no wider than it needs to be in order to keep it large in the window.

spell-kindle.note: The hearth mouth, the violet flame standing on bare firebrick and the unlit torch on the hearthstone. Full width survives; the crop spends the top of the chimney breast and the bottom hearth step, both of which the brief calls margin. Focal is the flame itself - the only thing on the page that is not cold.

spell-bulwark.note: The whole run of the dry-laid wall with the violet slip across its face, and the wreck piled against it: the splintered shafts, the near wheel, the spilled load and the draught chain snapped back on itself. The card keeps y 12.8%-88.2% and nothing is trimmed - the pad gives up the difference. What the top spends is the bank and the thorn above the coping, which is scenery; the coping itself is inside, and it has to be, because the argument of this card is that not one stone is out of place and a wall cut off at the window rule cannot say that. Focal on the face of the wall where the slip is, not on the wreck - the spell is what did NOT happen.

spell-cleanse.note: The washstand entire: the bowl with the water gone clear and the fouling settled hard-edged in the bottom of it, the wrung cloth on the rail, the fever-sheet folded square and dry, the unlit tallow candle. The ink fits exactly - the card keeps y 0.9%-76.3% and nothing named is cut. What the bottom loses is the jug on the shelf under the stand, which the brief never asked for. Focal on the clear water, which is where the violet slip is and the only place on this plate anything has happened.

spell-deep-draught.note: The brimming barrels with the water slopped over the chime and the violet slip on the near one, against the capped well: the boarded lid, the chain wound right up, the bucket bone dry on its hook, and the yoke and the two unused pails. 7.4% is spent off the BOTTOM (y 10.0%-85.5%), taking the feet of the barrels and some of the dark wet ground round them. That ground is named and it is a shame, but enough of it survives at the near barrel's foot to read, and the alternative was spending the top - which holds the chain and the dry bucket, and a Deep Draught with no dry bucket is a picture of some full barrels. Focal on the water standing in the near barrel's mouth.

spell-ember-lash.note: Both white-hot edges, the anvil face and the cold ash hafts running off to the top right. The crop spends the quench tub at the far left and the base of the stump; the raked-out fire bed stays in, because a dead forge is half of what this card is saying. Focal is the billhook's glowing curve, the strongest violet on the page.

spell-loft.note: The loaded wagon standing level on nothing, the ravine lip on both sides with the ruts running up to it and picking up again beyond, and the gap itself drawn plain - rock, air, and the thread of water a long way down. 7.0% is spent off the BOTTOM (y 8.0%-83.4%), taking the deepest part of the ravine. That is the right end to spend: what the card needs is that the drop is bottomless, not that the bottom is visible, and the water thread still runs out of the window rather than stopping in it. Focal on the empty air under the wheels, where the violet slip is, because the subject of this plate is a gap.

spell-mend-stone.note: The full run of the closing crack from hairline to sill end, the whole lintel, and the trowel set down clean on the sill. The crop spends the top course of the wall and the bottom step - the brief says the coursing may run to the margins. Focal is the middle of the crack rather than either end, because the card is about it closing, not about where it started.

event-strike.note: The yard at a dead stop: the cold furnace with its door open and the ash raked out, the row of barrows tipped up on their noses, the dead cooking fire, and the line of tools laid down straight across the gateway. Centred - the thumbnail keeps x 8.3%-91.7% - and the tool line is what settles that. It runs from 5% to 95% across and no window keeps it whole; centred, it runs out of BOTH edges, which reads as a line that continues, where a line held to one side reads as a line that stopped. What the thumbnail spends is one hammer at either end. Focal on the middle of the tool line, where the tongs are.

event-tax-levy.note: The trestle set square across the carriageway with the scales, the standard weights, the ledger and the inkwell on it, the strongbox chained to its leg, the second chest with its two locks behind, the rope on posts running out either side, and the carts backed up along the road. Held RIGHT: the thumbnail keeps x 15.7%-99.0%, which keeps both chests whole and spends the left-hand gatepost and its rope run. The rope survives on the right and says the same thing from one side; the chests do not repeat, and a levy with no strongbox in it is a weighbridge. Focal on the ledger and the inkwell in the middle of the table, where the actual transaction is.

event-train-heist.note: The van with its door run right back, the empty interior and the leaning ladder, with the locomotive kept whole at the left of the box - a half-drawn engine reads as an accident where a missing one does not. The thumbnail spends the cutting bank and the branch track, which the brief already calls margin. Focal is the open doorway.

event-piracy.note: The grounded hull with its mastheads, the trail of bales coming ashore, and the one small sail going away on the horizon at 87% across - which is what sets the right edge, because a piracy card without the ship that did it is a shipwreck card. The thumbnail spends the last of the open sea at either end. Focal is the hull.

event-smuggling-ring.note: The stacked kegs and bales, the boat dragged up the shingle and the shuttered lantern out on its rock at 87-95% across. Held right, so the thumbnail spends the outermost barrels rather than the lantern: the stack is a scatter and can lose a member, and the lantern is the only light in the picture and the only thing saying somebody is still here.

event-wolf-pack.note: The broken-through hurdle, the fleece caught in the split hazel, the single file of prints going away, and the crook with its lantern still burning at the right. Held right: the thumbnail takes a quarter off the far end of the hurdle lying flat, which still reads as a woven panel, rather than clipping the lantern. Focal is the gap in the fold.

character-chr-09.note: Odysseus squatting under the black hull with the coil across his knee, the marlinspike in his right hand and the sealed wine jar at his elbow. The ink runs 77.5% of the page against a card window that holds 73.4%, so 4.1% is spent and it goes off the BOTTOM - the crop keeps y 5.5%-78.9%. What that costs is his toes and the far ends of the scattered oarblades, which are sand and ground; this deck's own brief sets the lower margin aside for exactly that. Everything the card names is inside: the sheathed sword on its baldric at his left, the whole coil, the spike, and the jar down to its foot. Focal on the face, which is turned back over his shoulder - the card is a man listening to something behind him, and the eyes are the only part that says so.

character-chr-10.note: Eurylochus outside the door he will not go through: the head, the folded arms, the sheathed sword hanging past his knee, and the plank door ajar beside him. 6.1% cannot be kept and it is spent off the BOTTOM (y 10.5%-83.9%), which puts the dropped bronze cup - drawn at 85%-90% down the page - outside the window. That is the cheap loss and it was chosen: this deck's brief sets the lower margin aside for anything at the feet, the cup is the only named thing that fell into it, and the only way to buy it back was to cut his hair. The box starts about 2% above the crown so the head has air rather than sitting on the window rule. Focal on the face, which is turned at the door and not at us.

character-chr-11.note: Polites with his hand up to knock and his grin turned back over his shoulder, the sheathed sword and the ochre cloak, and the lion lying at the step with its head on its paws. 4.1% is spent off the BOTTOM (y 10.5%-83.9%) and it takes the toes of his boots and the outer flags of the threshold. The lion is whole, and it had to be: a young man knocking at a door is a picture of a young man, and the lion is the whole of what makes it Circe's house. Focal on the face.

character-chr-12.note: Perimedes kneeling to haul the lashing tight - both hands on the rope, the knife in his belt, the mast foot he is working against. The ink fits: the card keeps x 3.0%-97.0%, y 10.5%-79.7% and nothing named is cut. The wax comb and the ram's fleece are drawn at 79%-95% down the page, in the lower margin this deck's brief sets aside, and only the top of the fleece reaches the window; they are the offerings for the dead and worth naming here even though the picture spends them. Focal on the face, set in the effort - the rope runs off the top of the page, and a crop cannot aim at a line.

character-chr-13.note: Elpenor on the roof ridge rubbing the sleep out of his eyes, with the empty cup on the parapet beside him and the ladder leaning a little too far to his left. 1.1% is spent off the BOTTOM (y 4.5%-77.9%) and all it takes is the sole of one boot. Everything that tells the story is inside the window: the cup, the ladder he is going to miss, and the beached ship on the shore below to the right. Focal on the face - the card is a boy who has not woken up yet.

character-chr-14.note: Antiphus on the shingle with the oar under his arm, sorting cheeses out of the basket, the fleece heaped beside it and the cave mouth with its great flat stone small on the hill behind him. 2.8% is spent off the BOTTOM (y 9.5%-83.2%), taking the foot of the basket and his boots. What the TOP edge takes is the point of the grounded spear, drawn at 4% down the page: a spear is a line, a crop cannot aim at a line, and the point is the cheapest thing here - the shaft still runs the full height of the window and reads as a spear without it. Focal on the face, bent over the basket.

character-chr-15.note: Telemachus on the quay at dawn checking the strap of a sword he has not worn before, with the travelling bag on his shoulder, the lamp still burning in the doorway at the right, and the ship and the cloaked man small at the left. 1.1% is spent off the BOTTOM (y 5.5%-78.9%) and it takes his boots. The box starts about 2% above the crown so the head is not left standing on the window rule. Focal on the face, which is turned down onto his own hands - that is the card: a boy who has not done this before.

character-chr-16.note: Penelope unpicking the shroud: her hands and the small bronze pin at the loom, the finished cloth hanging in its fold behind her, the lamp and the cup on the stool at her left. This is the deepest trim in the deck - the ink runs 84.5% of the page against a window that holds 73.5%, so 11.0% goes, all of it off the BOTTOM (y 10.5%-84.0%). It buys the whole of the work: the hands, the pin, the warp, the fold of shroud. What it costs is the skirt of her dress and the foot of the wool basket in the corner, which keeps its rim and its wool. Focal on the face, in profile and looking at the thread rather than at us.

character-chr-17.note: Eumaeus at the gate of his sties cutting his own sandals out of the oxhide, four sows and their piglets about his feet, the boar-spear standing at the gatepost and the thatched hut small behind him. Everything survives but 0.2% (y 5.0%-78.3%), the spearhead at the top of the page included - which is why the box is drawn from 5% rather than down at his hair. What the bottom takes is the spread hide on the ground and the offcuts, which is the same material again and reads as ground. Focal on the face over the knife.

character-chr-18.note: Nausicaa wringing the linen at the river mouth, with the rest of it drying on the shingle behind her, the mule cart with its tailboard down at the right, and the olive bush at the left she is looking under. 9.6% is spent off the BOTTOM (y 7.0%-80.4%) and the leather ball, drawn at 78%-89% down the page, is what pays it: only its crown comes into the window. That was decided rather than allowed - the alternative was cutting her hair, which is the failure this file exists to stop, and a ball resting on the bottom edge still reads as a ball where a clipped head reads as a mistake. Focal on the face; she is looking off the left edge on purpose, because the brief put Odysseus under that bush.

character-chr-19.note: Circe at the great loom holding the two-handled cup out in both hands, the slender wand laid along the beam, the wolf lying across the threshold behind her, and the barley, the cheese and the honey jar on the table at the right. The ink fits and nothing named is cut (y 2.4%-75.9%). Worth saying out loud: the crop sits as high on the page as the box allows and her head still lands about 17% down the window rather than the 40% a focal point asks for. The plate has no paper above her - she is drawn with her hair at 7.5% of the page - and no box can buy back what was never drawn. What the bottom spends is her skirt and her sandals. Focal on the face.

character-chr-20.note: Calypso in the cave mouth turning the bronze axe-head over to test the edge, with the adze and the augur laid on the rock beside her, the springs running out below, and Odysseus far and small on his headland with his back to the cave. The ink fits: the card keeps x 0.0%-93.0%, y 12.5%-80.8%, and the 7% off the right is the focal sliding the window onto her - it costs open sea and nothing else. He is why the box runs out to 90% rather than stopping at the augur; the axe, the adze and the augur are the tools he leaves on, and the man looking away is what the card is about. Focal on her face, bent over the blade.

character-chr-21.note: Athena as Mentor, leaning in the doorway on the staff with one foot crossed over the other, watching the boy on the quay below. 6.1% is spent off the BOTTOM (y 10.5%-83.9%), taking the foot of the staff and the toes; the TOP edge takes the swallow on the lintel, drawn at 3%-8% down the page and out of reach of any box that also keeps the head whole. That is the decision here and it is the right way round - the card is the EYES, which are the one part of this figure that is not an old Ithacan, and a swallow at the top of the page is a grace note. Telemachus on the quay survives whole, which matters: who she is watching is half of who she is. Focal on the eyes, not on the middle of the face.

character-chr-22.note: Antinous sprawled in the carved chair at the head of the table, the gold cup halfway to his mouth and the footstool already in his other hand, the sword on the chair-back above him and the wreck of the feast running away to the right. 6.2% is spent off the BOTTOM (y 5.5%-78.8%), taking his boot and the bone on the floor. The box starts at the sword's pommel at 5.5% rather than at his hair, because a sword hung on somebody else's chair in somebody else's hall is the whole character in one object. Focal on the face - he is smiling.

event-boar-in-the-fields.note: The troughs ploughed through the standing barley, the hurdle smashed out of its posts and the cloven slots printed in the churned drinking place. The thumbnail spends the bramble at the far left and 2.2% off the outer edge of the wallow - the slots are well inside that. The scarecrow with its snapped crossbar survives whole. Focal is where the troughs meet the mud.

event-curdled-brew.note: The alembic cracked clean across the neck with its head lifted off and set down beside it, the tongue of set-hard contents stopped halfway to the floor over the bench edge, the scorched patch on the slate, and the rest of the glassware shoved back out of the way. Centred - the thumbnail keeps x 8.3%-91.7% - and everything named sits between 28% and 88%, so nothing is at risk. What both edges spend is more glassware, of which there is plenty. Focal on the body of the alembic just under the crack.

event-dragon-sighting.note: The abandoned hand cart with its load still roped on, the inn barred and benched, and the shadow band running edge to edge. The thumbnail spends the rock outcrop and half the stock crowded in the cleft - a herd is a scatter - and 0.6% off the far corner of the inn wall. Focal sits between the dropped shaft and the barred door, which are the two halves of the same sentence.

event-plague.note: The gate shut in daylight, the clean straw laid thick in front of it, the rope on its posts a few paces out, and the painted cross on the door of the nearest house. Held hard LEFT - the thumbnail keeps x 0.0%-83.3% - and that is the whole decision on this plate. The cross is at 2%-10% across and the abandoned barrow in the bare market square is at 78%-92%, so the two cannot both be in a window that keeps five sixths of the width. The cross wins: it is the sign the card is named for, and a barrow is a barrow. The card itself keeps the page and loses neither. Focal on the straw at the shut gate, between the two.

event-raiders.note: The spear driven in by the gatepost, the yard gate off both hinges and lying flat, and the timber stack pulled half across the entrance. Held LEFT, which is the opposite of most of this deck, because the spear is at 4% across and is the one object on the page that says armed band. The thumbnail spends the right end of the timber - a stack is a scatter - and grazes the jamb of the open door.

event-border-dispute.note: Both boundary marks, and nothing else could have set this box: the old stone is at 12% across and the new post at 88%, so the pair spans 77% of the page against a thumbnail that keeps 83%. One mark alone is a picture of a boundary; two is a picture of a dispute. Focal is the trodden ground between them where the two sets of ruts stop short of each other.
